Learning Objectives
Review massive rotator cuff tears.
Review classification systems associated with massive rotator cuff tears.
Identify appropriate indications for superior capsule reconstruction.
Describe preoperative planning for the management of massive rotator cuff tears.
Explain the technique for the management of massive rotator cuff tears.
Discuss the postoperative rehabilitation plan after the management of massive rotator cuff
tears.
Review the outcomes of superior capsule reconstruction.

Pathoanatomy
Overview
Although partial repair is associated with positive short-term results, results deteriorate within
a few years.1
Tendon transfers are limited in their ability to restore overhead motion.2
Recently reverse shoulder arthroplasty has become more commonly used to manage
irreparable rotator cuff tears, especially in elderly patients.
However, it is associated with a high complication rate in younger patients (<65 years).3
In addition, reverse shoulder arthroplasty in patients with a massive cuff tear without
substantial limitations in range of motion (ROM) results in less-than-optimal outcomes.4
The procedure has been shown to restore joint mechanics (translation and subacromial
pressure) biomechanically and has demonstrated improvement in functional outcomes in
properly selected patients.5
Some controversy exists with regard to the selection of autograft or allograft sources; long-
term studies are necessary to further evaluate outcomes.

Overview
The prevalence of rotator cuff tears increases with age, with a risk of bilateral tears as
high as 50% in individuals 66 years or older.6 Massive rotator cuff tears may be
categorized according to size—greater than 5 cm—or as a complete tear of at least two
tendons.7 These tears may lead to substantial pain and dysfunction and often progress
to rotator cuff arthropathy because of loss of force couples.8
Most massive rotator cuff tears can be repaired via a combination of arthroscopic
techniques.9 Various techniques, such as capsular release and interval slides, can be
used to aid in mobilization.
Although factors such as grade 3 Goutallier changes increase the risk of irreparability
and/or subsequent repair failure, no one sign is predictive of irreparability. Conversely,
the risk of complete repair decreases with massive tears, particularly those with grade 3

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075

Goutallier changes10 and in which previous repair failed.11 Poor-quality tissue can be
managed via alternative fixation strategies, such as rip-stop configurations; however,
poor biology remains a limiting factor (Resources 1 and 2).
In young patients with an irreparable cuff tear, treatment options have historically
included partial repair, tendon transfer, or arthroplasty.12
In this setting, superior capsule reconstruction (SCR) has emerged as a potential joint-
preserving option to treat young patients who have an irreparable, massive rotator cuff
tear without glenohumeral arthritis.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy
Histologically, the rotator cuff has been described as having up to five distinct layers.13
The superior capsule is the deepest layer (layer five), lies beneath the supraspinatus and
infraspinatus tendons, and ranges in width from 9 to 26 mm.14
The origin is thickest near the base of the coracoid anteriorly and near the scapular spine
posteriorly.15
The insertion spans the medial aspect of the greater tuberosity and occupies almost 50% of
the tuberosity from medial to lateral.15
The vascular supply to the capsule comes medially from the glenoid and laterally from the
greater tuberosity. Additional vascular supply is provided by vessels from the rotator cuff
that perforate the capsule superiorly.16 This pattern may be relevant to graft healing, which,
in the absence of a rotator cuff, requires creeping vascularization from the medial and lateral
aspects.
Biomechanics
Dermal allografting results in partial restoration of superior translation and complete
restoration of subacromial contact pressure, but it does not restore stability as well as a TFL
graft.5
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Massive Rotator Cuff Tears and Superior Capsule Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
3/22

The stability of SCR is improved with the addition of posterior margin convergence sutures to
the remaining intact rotator cuff.17

Biomechanics
Although the rotator cuff provides dynamic stability to the glenohumeral joint during
early and middle ROM, the shoulder capsule provides static restraint at the end points of
ROM. Biomechanical research has demonstrated that a defect in the superior capsule
leads to increased superior translation.18 Loss of the superior capsule and the rotator
cuff (particularly the infraspinatus) may lead to loss of stabilization and superior
translation because of an unopposed deltoid force on the proximal humerus.18
SCR has the potential to restore superior stability to the glenohumeral joint. Mihata et
al5 demonstrated that securing a tensor fascia lata (TFL) graft to the glenoid and the
greater tuberosity diminished superior translation to native levels in a massive rotator
cuff tear model.
Natural History
Zingg et al19 examined the natural history of the progression of massive cuff tears. Patients
with a larger tear (involving more tendons) showed a higher progression of osteoarthritis
compared with patients with a smaller tear at 4-year follow-up. An overall increase in tear size,
progression of fatty infiltration by a mean of one stage in three muscles, and a decrease in
acromiohumeral distance (AHD) were noted at final follow-up. One-half of the eight rotator
cuff tears graded as reparable at the beginning of the study were graded as irreparable at final
follow-up.

Natural History
Many studies have reported on the ability of full-thickness rotator cuff tears to progress
in size during short-term follow-up.20 Dissimilar from acute injuries, massive rotator cuff
tears more commonly result from chronic degenerative changes and are associated with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Massive Rotator Cuff Tears and Superior Capsule Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
4/22

tendon retraction, loss of muscle elasticity, and fatty muscle infiltration.12 The natural
history of massive rotator cuff tears is that of progression of superior migration and
glenohumeral degenerative changes.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Helpful to distinguish between patients who are limited by pain (elucidated via injection or
passive raising the arm to 90° and testing to see if the patient can hold the arm at that level)
and patients with functional limitations
Although recovery of pseudoparalysis after primary repair may be as high as 90% in acute
cases, the likelihood of recovery decreases with chronic pseudoparalysis or in the revision
setting.11,21
SCR has been reported to reverse pseudoparalysis;8 however, true anterosuperior escape
typically is more chronic in nature and difficult to manage via a joint preservation procedure.
Several physical examination tests can be used to define the tear pattern and prognosis for
recovery.
Inability to maintain external rotation with the arm in 20° of abduction and maximal external
rotation is considered a positive external rotation lag sign and has been reported to be
associated with a sensitivity of 65% for the detection of lesions that extend into the
infraspinatus tendon.22
Walch et al23 reported that inability to maintain external rotation with the arm at the side
(dropping sign) and inability to externally rotate the arm from a position of 90° abduction
with the elbow flexed 90° (Hornblower sign) are associated with a sensitivity of 100% for the
detection of grade 3 or grade 4 fatty degeneration of the infraspinatus and teres minor
muscles.
A Hornblower sign is a poor prognostic factor for SCR and is best managed via tendon
transfer or reverse shoulder arthroplasty with tendon transfer according to patient age and
severity of arthritis.
The bear hug test has been reported to be associated with the highest sensitivity for the
detection of subscapularis tendon tears.24 Given the inaccuracy of MRI in detecting
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Massive Rotator Cuff Tears and Superior Capsule Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
5/22

subscapularis tendon tears,23 a positive bear hug test should alert surgeons to a previously
missed subscapularis tear.
Findings of the lift-off test may not be positive until a tear is 75% or more of the length of the
subscapularis tendon.24

Physical Examination
A complete shoulder examination includes an inspection for muscle atrophy, scapular
winging, and prior surgical scars; complete assessment of ROM; strength testing; a
neurovascular examination of the affected extremity; and special testing as necessary. In
addition, the clinician should assess for pseudoparalysis, defined by most studies as
active elevation of less than 90° with full passive ROM.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Plain radiographs are used to assess the glenohumeral joint space (more than 2 mm joint
space remaining), evaluate for proximal migration, and evaluate for adaptive changes of the
proximal humerus (ie, femoralization) and the undersurface of the acromion (ie,
acetabularization).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating the rotator cuff. MRIs should be
scrutinized for tear size, tendon retraction, tendon length, and fatty infiltration.
Sheean et al9 reported on radiographic factors associated with repairability in 86 massive
rotator cuff tears managed via arthroscopic repair. Complete repair was achieved in 88% of
the rotator cuff tears, including 82% of the rotator cuff tears (9 of 11) with an AHD of less
than 7 mm, 70% of the rotator cuff tears (14 of 20) with a positive tangent sign, and 57% of
the rotator cuff tears (8 of 14) with grade 3 or grade 4 fatty infiltration of the supraspinatus.
Advanced mobilization techniques (interval slides) were used in 62% of the rotator cuff tears.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
6/22

Kim et al25 reported that individual signs alone, such as the tangent sign, were not
completely predictive of an irreparable rotator cuff tear. In their experience, the best
predictor of an irreparable rotator cuff tear was infraspinatus fatty infiltration higher than
grade 2 and retraction of the tendon to the level of glenoid (odds ratio, 127; sensitivity, 54%).
CT or Ultrasonography
CT arthrography and ultrasonography are reserved for patients in whom MRI is
contraindicated.
Ultrasonography
Less expensive than MRI but highly operator dependent
Not conducive to assessment of muscle quality
CT arthrography
Can be used to assess tear size and muscle quality
Requires injection of intra-articular contrast, which is not always well tolerated by the
patient
Classification
Cofield described massive rotator cuff tears according to size.26
Small: < 2 cm
Medium: 1 to 3 cm
Large: 3 to 5 cm
Massive: >5 cm
Hamada first described the radiographic findings of massive rotator cuff tears in 1990.
The classification provides a mechanical theory for the radiographic changes observed in the
progression to rotator cuff arthropathy.27
This reflects the chronicity of a rotator cuff tear and has been associated with outcomes after
SCR, with grade 1 and grade 2 being most amenable to SCR.21
Grade 1: preserved acromiohumeral interval
Grade 2: decreased acromiohumeral interval without adaptive changes of the proximal
humerus
Grade 3: adaptive changes (acetabularization of the acromion or rounding of the greater
tuberosity)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075

Grade 4: glenohumeral joint space narrowing
Grade 5: humeral head collapse27
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management should be considered for irreparable rotator cuff tears.
Zingg et al19 evaluated 19 massive rotator tears managed nonsurgically, with a mean follow-
up of 48 months, and reported a mean Constant-Murley score of 83% and a subjective
shoulder value of 68%.
From initial management to follow-up, glenohumeral arthritis progressed, tear size
increased, AHD decreased, and fatty infiltration increased.
Given this progression, a nonsurgical treatment approach is reserved for two types of
patients.
Older patients in whom an arthroplasty procedure is acceptable if nonsurgical treatment
fails
Patients who are poor candidates for joint preservation techniques because of medical
comorbidities19 (Resources 3, 4 and 5).
Surgical Management

Surgical Management
In the initial description of the technique by Mihata et al,5 a TFL autograft was used. The
graft was attached medially to the glenoid with the use of two anchors and laterally to
the greater tuberosity with the use of four anchors. In the United States, the technique
was adapted to use dermal allograft to avoid donor site morbidity.5
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Massive Rotator Cuff Tears and Superior Capsule Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
8/22

Although indications for this procedure are narrow, SCR is considered primarily if the aim is
joint preservation, a goal based on lack of arthritis or younger age. The American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons evidence-based clinical practice guideline on the management of
rotator cuff injuries states that that SCR is one option for irreparable rotator cuff tears, among
many treatment options, with no one treatment option demonstrating superiority. Ideal
candidates have the following characteristics:
Age younger than 70 years
Good health
Nonsmoker
Irreparable rotator cuff tear with minimal to no arthritis (Hamada grade 1 or grade 2)
Intact or repairable subscapularis tendon
Contraindications
Advanced adaptive changes of the humeral head or the acromion or advanced glenohumeral
arthritis (Hamada grade 3 or 4)
Uncontrolled diabetes mellitus
Subscapularis tear with grade 3 changes
Lack of external rotation at the side or a Hornblower sign
Active infection
Brachial plexus or axillary nerve injury
Autoimmune disorders or use of disease-modifying drugs that affect healing 
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
The surgeon must be prepared for repair and SCR, depending on intraoperative findings.
Patient Positioning
Lateral decubitus or beach-chair position
The graft should be secured in 20° to 30° of abduction.
Surgical Approaches
The basic steps of the procedure are as follows:

Perform diagnostic arthroscopy.
Address biceps and subscapularis pathology if present.
Prepare bone beds.
Place glenoid and medial tuberosity anchors.
Size and prepare the graft.
Shuttle the graft and then secure it to the glenoid.
Secure the graft to the tuberosity.
Perform side-to-side reinforcement of the graft.
The following describes an arthroscopic approach in the lateral decubitus position28:
First, a standard posterolateral viewing portal is established.
The subscapularis tendon is visualized and repaired, if necessary, before the procedure.
The tendon is managed according to pathology findings; if it is diseased or unstable, it can
undergo tenotomy or tenodesis.
A biceps tenotomy or tenodesis also may be performed in patients with disruption of the
medial sling; if the tendon is intact, it typically is not managed. Although controversial, the
biceps tendon may assist as a restraint against superior migration of the humeral head.
Limited subacromial decompression is performed.
Bony landmarks, such as the scapular spine and the undersurface of the acromioclavicular
joint, are dissected out and fully visualized.
Next, three anchors are placed in the superior glenoid neck for medial fixation.
The bone bed of the superior glenoid is prepared with the use of a motorized shaver and
ring curettes. Three anchors are placed into the glenoid, ideally in the 10-o’clock, 12-o’clock,
and 2-o’clock positions, as follows:
The anterior anchor is placed through a modified anterosuperior portal just anterior to
the acromioclavicular joint.
The posterior anchor is placed through an accessory portal along the posterior margin of
the acromion.
The central anchor typically is placed through a Neviaser portal.
If the anterior and posterior anchors are placed 2 to 3 mm medial to the glenoid labrum,
the superior labrum can be preserved to optimize the contact area between graft and
bone.
Attention is then turned toward the greater tuberosity. The bone bed is prepared. A double-
row repair construct is preferred for lateral fixation.

9/3/26, 4:38 PM

10/22

First, two medial row anchors are placed into the tuberosity, with the anterior anchor placed
just posterior to the bicipital groove and the posterior anchor placed at the posterior aspect
of the defect.
A calibrated probe is used to precisely measure the size of the defect to be spanned and the
distance between each anchor.
Because the measurements will dictate graft tension, the arm is placed in 20° to 30°
abduction and 20° of forward flexion.
An acellular dermal allograft is cut to size, and the exact positions of each anchor are
marked.
The graft is oversized by 5 mm in the medial, anterior, and posterior aspects to ensure
extra overhang of the graft for suturing into the adjacent intact cuff.
Laterally, the graft is oversized by 10 mm to establish overlap over the footprint; this will
aid in graft incorporation.
Although findings of a biomechanical cadaver model study demonstrated substantially
improved glenohumeral superior translation, subacromial peak contact pressure, and
cumulative deltoid force with the use of a 6-mm graft compared with a 3-mm graft, no
clinical evidence showed that a 6 mm graft was superior.29 Most reports in the literature
have described the use of a 3-mm graft.
The sutures from the five anchors are shuttled through the lateral portal, with care taken to
not entangle them. Each set of sutures is then individually shuttled through the graft with the
use of a suture passer.
If using knotless anchors, the glenoid sutures may be individually passed through the graft in
an inverted mattress fashion to maximize fixation on the glenoid (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration of a shoulder shows graft shuttling via an anchor-based technique. The
graft can be pulled in via the glenoid anchors (knotless technique shown) and by pushing
with the use of an instrument from the lateral portal. A flexible silicone cannula that has
been pre-split helps the graft pass into the shoulder and can be removed from around the
sutures if the graft is too big to pass easily. (Reproduced from Duquin TR, Hohman DW Jr,
Hartzler RU: Arthroscopic rotator cuff repair, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential
Orthopaedic Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2020, pp 205-217.)
For humeral fixation, a double-pulley technique is used.
A suture limb from the anterior and posterior humeral anchors is selected and tied over the
instrument and cut short.
The graft is pushed into the joint, and the slack is removed from the glenoid anchors.
The dermal allograft is delivered to the tuberosity.
The two free limbs on the humeral side are then tied together.

The suture limb tapes from the medial row of tuberosity anchors are crisscrossed and fixed
laterally to the humerus with the use of knotless anchors (Figure 2).

Finally, if possible, the supraspinatus is repaired in side-to-side fashion to the infraspinatus
over the graft. Marginal convergence sutures are placed between the graft and the intact
rotator cuff so the remaining rotator cuff overlies the graft (Video 1).

Postoperative Management
The portals are closed, and a soft dressing is placed.
The arm is placed in a sling for 6 weeks to restrict shoulder motion.
Postoperative management is based on surgeon discretion.
Complications
A low rate of complications has been reported with this procedure.
Denard et al11 reported a complication rate of 6.8% with dermal allograft.
In the first study by Mihata et al,30 no complications occurred at final follow-up.
In a systematic review on SCR for massive irreparable cuff tears, the most common
complication was graft re-tear (13%).31
Other possible complications include infection, stiffness/contracture, or anchor pullout.
Rehabilitation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:38 PM
AAOS | Massive Rotator Cuff Tears and Superior Capsule Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002075
14/22

A sling is worn for 6 weeks postoperatively; it may be removed for showering and care
activities, such as changing clothes. Hand, wrist, and elbow ROM is allowed immediately
postoperatively.
Passive shoulder ROM exercises are initiated at 6 weeks postoperatively and progress to active
assisted exercises.
Strengthening is delayed until 16 weeks postoperatively.
Unrestricted use of the shoulder is avoided for 6 to 12 months postoperatively to facilitate
graft incorporation.

Rehabilitation
Postoperative stiffness is rare after massive irreparable cuff repair. Therefore, emphasis
is placed on healing, keeping in mind that graft integration may take longer than healing
after standard cuff repair.21
Outcomes
Mihata et al32 reported the first clinical series on SCR.
A cohort of 24 patients underwent SCR with TFL autograft and partial cuff repair, with a mean
follow-up of 31 months. Active shoulder elevation improved by 64°, and active external
rotation improved by 14°. AHD improved from 4.6 mm preoperatively to 8.7 mm
postoperatively.
Graft healing was observed in 83% of the patients. Mean American Shoulder and Elbow
Society (ASES) scores drastically improved from 24 preoperatively to 93 postoperatively.
Postoperative MRI demonstrated healing in 83% of the grafts.
Mihata et al33 later reported on the 5-year outcomes of SCR.
The authors assessed 30 shoulders. ASES Shoulder Scores and Japanese Orthopaedic
Association Scores improved substantially at 1 year and 5 years. ASES scores at 1 year and 5
years after SCR were better in healed patients than in unhealed patients with a graft tear.
In addition, patients with an intact graft had preservation of the glenohumeral joint, whereas
those who experienced failed graft healing had progression of arthritis.

Denard et al21 reviewed SCR with the use of dermal allograft in 59 patients at a mean 1-year
follow-up.
Patient satisfaction was 72.9%, and 62.9% of patients had returned to normal activity. The
highest success rate was observed in patients with Hamada grade 1 or grade 2 arthritis.
Complete graft healing was observed in only 45% of the patients. The patients with complete
graft healing had the most successful outcomes, with lower pain levels and higher ASES
scores.
Pennington et al34 reported on arthroscopic SCR with the use of dermal allograft.
86 patients were evaluated at a mean follow-up of 1 year. The mean AHD increased from 7.1
mm preoperatively to 9.7 mm postoperatively.
Mean increases in forward flexion from 120° to 160° and in abduction from 103° to 159°
were reported.
Patients reported a 90% satisfaction rate.
Burkhart et al35 reported on the 2-year outcomes of arthroscopic SCR with the use of dermal
allograft.
33 patients were evaluated with a mean follow-up of 34 months. ASES scores improved from
52 preoperatively to 90 postoperatively. External rotation improved by a mean of 11° at final
follow-up.
85% of the grafts fully healed. A 19% rate of unsatisfactory outcomes was reported.
AHD improved from 7 mm to 8 mm.
Lacheta et al36 reported the 2-year outcomes of arthroscopic SCR with the use of dermal
allograft.
22 patients were assessed at a mean follow-up of 2.1 years.
85% of the patients exceeded the minimum clinically important difference in ASES scores.
Radiographs demonstrated a mean increase in AHD from 7 mm to 8.3 mm in 86% of the
patients.
No substantial differences in clinical outcomes were observed between those with an intact
graft and those with graft failure. One clinical failure was reported.
Pearls and Pitfalls
The ideal indication is a younger patient without substantial glenohumeral arthritis (Hamada
grade 1 and grade 2) who has a massive, irreparable rotator cuff tear.

The subscapularis must be intact or repaired in combination with SCR to balance force
couples28,30
Graft tension at the time of sizing is optimized with approximately 20° to 30° of abduction.7
Independent medial anchors provide improved biomechanical stability.
The graft must be sutured posteriorly to the infraspinatus to re-create stability.7,37
